subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

textbook_items_in_class.description: Measure the lengths of a pen, sharpener, and an object of the student's choice using a scale; record the measurements in centimetres using tenth notation as modelled in the section.
Write lengths of objects (USB cable, and others shown in diagrams) in two ways — as a mixed number and as an improper tenth fraction — and read them aloud.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.2 p.49
textbook_items_in_class.description: Arrange eight lengths in increasing order: (a) 9/10; (b) 1 7/10; (c) 130/10; (d) 13 1/10; (e) 10 5/10; (f) 7 6/10; (g) 6 7/10; (h) 4/10.

homework.description: Arrange four lengths in increasing order: 4 1/10, 4/10, 41/10, 41 1/10.

time_bands.activity: Pose the Sonu screw puzzle from section 3.1: two screws look the same but differ by a fraction of a centimetre. Students discuss in pairs why a whole-centimetre reading on a ruler cannot settle which screw is longer. The class surfaces the need for a finer unit.

Work through Figure it Out, section 3.1 p.47 ("Measure the lengths of a pen, sharpener, and an object..."). Students place each object on a millimetre-ruled scale and record measurements as mixed numbers such as 2 7/10 cm, practising the tenth-notation the section models.

Introduce section 3.2's pencil-length diagram: 34 one-tenths equal three full units plus four tenths. Students complete Figure it Out, section 3.2 p.49 ("Write lengths of objects..."), writing each length as both a mixed number and an improper tenth fraction, then reading measurements aloud.

Students arrange the eight tenth-fraction lengths in Figure it Out Q1, section 3.2 p.49 ("Arrange eight lengths in increasing order...") by converting each to a single improper fraction and comparing. A brief whole-class check follows.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who write 1 7/10 as 17/10 correctly but then treat 130/10 as thirteen-and-zero-tenths; the denominator 10 means the entire numerator is in tenths. Measuring with a physical ruler before writing fractions connects the concrete object to the notation and reduces this slip. Figure it Out, section 3.2 p.50 is a useful extension for students who finish early.
materials: one additional small classroom object per student

periods.activity_title: Adding and Subtracting Tenth Lengths in Context

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the total length of a honeybee given head = 2 3/10 units, thorax = 5 4/10 units, abdomen = 7 5/10 units.
Find the length of Shylaja's middle finger given total hand length 12 4/10 units and palm length 6 7/10 units; discuss two methods shown and try computing by converting to tenths.
Find the difference in lengths between a Celestial Pearl Danio (2 4/10 cm) and a Philippine Goby (9/10 cm); compare to finger size.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.2 p.52
textbook_items_in_class.description: Observe six sequences of tenth-fractions, identify the change after each term, and extend each pattern by four more terms: (a) 4, 4 3/10, 4 6/10, …; (b) 8 2/10, 8 7/10, 9 2/10, …; (c) 7 6/10, 8 7/10, …; (d) 5 7/10, 5 3/10, …; (e) 13 5/10, 13, 12 5/10, …; (f) 11 5/10, 10 4/10, 9 3/10, …

time_bands.activity: Revisit the two methods for adding tenth fractions (units-and-tenths column method vs. convert-all-to-tenths) from the section 3.2 guided computation. Work through Figure it Out, section 3.2 p.51 ("Find the total length of a honeybee...") as a class demonstration, showing both approaches.

Students work independently on Figure it Out, section 3.2 p.51 ("Find the length of Shylaja's middle finger...") and Figure it Out, section 3.2 p.52 ("Find the difference in lengths between a Celestial Pearl Danio..."). They compare both methods and decide which they find more efficient.

Groups of three work on Figure it Out Q1, section 3.2 p.52 ("Observe six sequences of tenth-fractions..."), identifying the constant change in each sequence and writing four more terms. Groups share one sequence each, explaining the pattern in words before writing it.

periods.teacher_notes: The regrouping step in subtraction (e.g., 12 4/10 – 6 7/10) is the most common site of error: students subtract 4 from 7 without regrouping a unit. Encourage students to convert to tenths first as a check. Figure it Out Q1, section 3.2 p.52 builds pattern-recognition alongside the arithmetic, so both goals are served simultaneously.

periods.activity_title: Folding to a Hundredth — Building the New Unit

textbook_items_in_class.description: How many one-hundredths make one-tenth? Can the folded-paper length also be stated as 4 units and 45 one-hundredths? Explain.
Fill the empty boxes in the ruler diagram: given markings at 0, 1/10, 1/100, 2/10, 20/100, 1, 99/100, 130/100, 3/10, 2, identify the missing decimal lengths at each marked position.
For lengths shown in the diagrams, write each measurement in decimal fraction form and read the measurement aloud in words (sample answers: 5 37/100 and 15 3/100 shown in the teacher answer key).

time_bands.activity: Students fold a strip of paper in half, measure the result and discover the half-length cannot be expressed with tenths alone. The class discusses Math Talk, section 3.3 p.53 ("How many one-hundredths make one-tenth?..."), establishing that each tenth splits into 10 parts giving 100 parts per unit.

Students work through Figure it Out, section 3.3 p.54 ("Fill the empty boxes in the ruler diagram..."), placing tenths and hundredths on the same number line and writing equivalent representations (e.g., 2/10 = 20/100). The wire-diagram example from the section is shown to reinforce multiple representations of the same length.

Students complete Figure it Out, section 3.3 p.54 ("For lengths shown in the diagrams, write each measurement in decimal fraction form..."), writing each diagram length as a mixed tenths-and-hundredths fraction and reading it aloud. Pairs check each other's verbal readings for precision.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse 3/10 and 3/100 when writing them on the same ruler, placing both at the same position. Use the ruler diagram to make explicit that 3/10 = 30/100 — the hundredths ruler needs 30 steps to reach the same point that the tenths ruler reaches in 3. Figure it Out Q1, section 3.3 p.55 extends the comparison work if time permits.
materials: strips of paper (one per student) for folding

periods.activity_title: Column Arithmetic with Tenths and Hundredths

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.3 p.55
textbook_items_in_class.description: In seven groups (a)–(g), identify the longest and shortest length from the given set of tenths and hundredths values, and mark each length on the scale: (a) 3/10, 3/100, 33/100; (b) 3 1/10, 30/10, 1 3/10; (c) 45/100, 54/100, 5/10, 4/10; (d) 3 6/10, 3 6/100, 3 6/10 6/100; (e) 8 2/100, 9/100, 1 8/100; (f) 7 3/10 5/100, 7 5/10, 7 41/100; (g) 65/10 15/100, 5 87/100, 5 7/100.
Solve by converting to hundredths: find the difference 25 9/10 – 6 4/10 7/100; then find 15 3/10 4/100 – 2 6/10 8/100 and observe structural similarity with whole-number column subtraction 653 – 268.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.3 p.58

time_bands.activity: Students compare groups of lengths in Figure it Out Q1, section 3.3 p.55 ("In seven groups (a)–(g), identify the longest and shortest length...") by converting all values to hundredths. After independent work, pairs share their number-line markings to check for consistent placement.

Work through Math Talk, section 3.3 p.57 ("Solve by converting to hundredths: find the difference 25 9/10 – 6 4/10 7/100...") as a class, placing digits in a units-tenths-hundredths column layout and comparing the result to the analogous whole-number subtraction 653 – 268. Students articulate the structural parallel aloud.

Students complete Figure it Out Q1, section 3.3 p.58 ("Find sums and differences of mixed tenths-and-hundredths numbers..."), showing full column working. The teacher circulates to catch misaligned columns and reinforce that tenths align with tenths, hundredths with hundredths.

periods.teacher_notes: The single most common error here is adding a tenths digit to a hundredths digit because the student did not align columns; holding the place value column header visible on the board throughout the exercise prevents most misalignments. Structural similarity with whole-number column arithmetic (observed in Math Talk, section 3.3 p.57) is worth making explicit — it shows students they are applying a familiar algorithm, not learning a new one.
materials: place value column template drawn on board

periods.activity_title: Why Ten? Extending the Place Value Chain

textbook_items_in_class.description: Discuss: could 4 2/10 be written as 42 skipping the fraction denominator? What ambiguity arises? Show three different quantities that could all be denoted '705' without a positional separator.

How Big? Answer: (a) how many thousandths make one unit; (b) how many thousandths make one tenth; (c) how many thousandths make one hundredth; (d) how many tenths make one ten; (e) how many hundredths make one ten. Then make a few more similar questions and answer them.

Make a place value table (hundreds, tens, units, tenths, hundredths, thousandths). Write each quantity in decimal form, place value expansion, and read aloud: (a) 2 ones, 3 tenths, 5 hundredths; (b) 1 ten and 5 tenths; (c) 4 ones and 6 hundredths; (d) 1 hundred, 1 one and 1 hundredth; (e) 8/100 and 9/10; (f) 5/100; (g) 1/10; (h) 2 1/100, 4 1/10, 7 1/1000.

homework.description: Write in decimal form: (a) 234 hundredths; (b) 105 tenths.

time_bands.activity: Open with Math Talk, section 3.4 p.61 ("Discuss: could 4 2/10 be written as 42 skipping the fraction denominator?..."), tracing the full place value chain from ten-thousands down through units, then extending it rightward to tenths, hundredths and thousandths. Students justify in their own words why splitting by 10 is consistent with the Indian base-ten system.

Students answer Figure it Out, section 3.4 p.61 ("How Big?...") individually, quantifying relationships across the place value chain. They then write two self-generated questions in the same format and swap with a partner to answer.

Students construct the full place value table (hundreds through thousandths) and complete Figure it Out, section 3.4 p.63 ("Make a place value table..."), writing each quantity in decimal notation, as a place value expansion, and reading each aloud. The teacher introduces section 3.5 measurement conversions (1 mm = 0.1 cm, 1 cm = 0.01 m) as direct applications of the place value table just built.

periods.teacher_notes: The deductive pivot is the argument from place value structure: because each position is ten times the one to its right, the decimal point notation is forced — not arbitrary. Students who can articulate this argument make far fewer place value errors in section 3.5. Watch for the misconception that 0.1 and 0.01 are 'basically the same' — the place value table makes the ten-fold difference immediately visible.
materials: place value table template (hundreds to thousandths) on board or printed sheet

periods.activity_title: Decimal Numbers on the Line — Measure, Locate, and Compute

textbook_items_in_class.description: Fill in the blanks for mm ↔ cm conversions: 70 mm = ___ cm; ___ = 0.9 cm; 134 mm = ___; ___ = 203.6 cm.
Zero Dilemma: Sonu says 0.2 = 0.20 = 0.200. Zara disagrees. Use the place value table to settle the dispute; then determine which of 4.5, 4.05, 0.405, 4.050, 4.50, 4.005, 04.50 are equal.
Which decimal number is greater? (a) 1.23 or 1.32; (b) 3.81 or 13.800; (c) 1.009 or 1.090.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.7 p.75
Figure it Out Q2, section 3.7 p.75

time_bands.activity: Students complete Figure it Out, section 3.5 p.64 ("Fill in the blanks for mm ↔ cm conversions...") applying the conversion 1 mm = 0.1 cm derived from the place value chain. The teacher draws out the analogous g ↔ kg and paise ↔ rupee ratios quickly, showing all three conversion families as place value shifts.

Introduce number-line location from section 3.6: subdivide the unit interval into 10 parts to place 1.4, then zoom in further for three-place decimals. Address Math Talk, section 3.6 p.70 ("Zero Dilemma: Sonu says 0.2 = 0.20 = 0.200...") using a place value table on the board — trailing zeros do not change value, but leading zeros after the decimal point do.

Students complete Figure it Out, section 3.6 p.73 ("Which decimal number is greater?...") using left-to-right digit comparison, mirroring the whole-number procedure. A quick partner check ensures agreement on all three comparisons.

Students work through Figure it Out Q1, section 3.7 p.75 ("Find the sums...") and Figure it Out Q2, section 3.7 p.75 ("Find the differences...") using decimal column form, aligning decimal points. The teacher circulates to ensure students append trailing zeros when operands have different decimal lengths (e.g., 18 written as 18.000 when subtracting 8.8).

periods.teacher_notes: Aligning the decimal points in column arithmetic is the direct extension of aligning place values in whole-number arithmetic — reinforcing this connection prevents the single most common procedural error in section 3.7. The Zero Dilemma discussion (Math Talk, section 3.6 p.70) is worth holding as a whole-class conversation because students who believe 0.20 > 0.2 will make systematic comparison errors in section 3.8.

periods.activity_title: When Decimals Mislead — Errors, Boundaries, and History

textbook_items_in_class.description: Where else can we see 'non-decimal' numbers written with a decimal-like notation? (The cricket overs and feet-inches examples are given; students generate further instances.)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.8 p.78
textbook_items_in_class.description: Convert fractions into decimals: (a) 5/100; (b) 16/1000; (c) 12/10; (d) 254/1000.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 3.8 p.79
textbook_items_in_class.description: Will a decimal number with more digits necessarily be greater than one with fewer digits? Justify with an example.

Evaluate Sonu's claim that the sum of two decimal numbers always lies strictly between (sum of whole-number parts) and (sum of whole-number parts + 2). Verify for 25.936 + 8.202 and for 25.93603259 + 8.202.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 3.8 p.79
homework.description: Mahi buys 0.25 kg beans, 0.3 kg carrots, 0.5 kg potatoes, 0.2 kg capsicums, 0.05 kg ginger. Calculate total weight.

time_bands.activity: Present the three real-world disaster vignettes from section 3.8: the Air Canada Boeing 767 fuel miscalculation (pounds vs. kilograms), the Amsterdam housing-benefit overpayment (€188 million), and the medical dosing error (0.05 mg vs. 0.5 mg). Students discuss in pairs what decimal error caused each incident and what the correct reading should have been.

Address Math Talk, section 3.8 p.78 ("Where else can we see 'non-decimal' numbers written with a decimal-like notation?...") using cricket overs (base 6) and feet-and-inches (base 12) as opening examples. Students generate further instances — time (hours and minutes), degrees and minutes of angle — and the class reasons why these look like but are not true base-ten decimals.

Students complete Figure it Out Q1, section 3.8 p.78 ("Convert fractions into decimals...") and Figure it Out Q6, section 3.8 p.79 ("Will a decimal number with more digits necessarily be greater?..."), producing a written justification with a counterexample. The historical timeline (8th-century Indian astronomers, al-Uqlīdisī 950 CE, 15th–16th century European notations) is sketched briefly on the board.

Students work on Math Talk, section 3.7 p.76 ("Evaluate Sonu's claim that the sum of two decimal numbers always lies strictly between..."), verifying the claim for the two given sums and articulating in writing whether the claim holds — connecting addition arithmetic back to reasoning about bounds.

periods.teacher_notes: The key reasoning goal is that decimal notation is meaningful only when the base is ten — cricket overs and feet-inches use a similar separator but their arithmetic is not decimal. Students who can construct and explain a counterexample for Figure it Out Q6, section 3.8 p.79 demonstrate genuine understanding of place value. Figure it Out Q4, section 3.8 p.79 on descending order is a useful self-study item for students who wish further practice with comparison.

items.prompt: A student measures a pencil on a centimetre ruler and records its length as somewhere between 7 cm and 8 cm. Which of the following statements best explains why a whole-centimetre reading is insufficient for this measurement?

options.label: A
options.text: Centimetre rulers are not accurate enough to measure pencils.

options.label: B
options.text: The pencil is too long to be measured in centimetres.

options.label: C
options.text: The pencil length falls between two whole-centimetre marks, so a smaller unit is needed to record it precisely.

options.label: D
options.text: Whole-centimetre numbers can only describe objects longer than 10 cm.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option B. When a length falls between two whole-centimetre marks, recording only whole centimetres loses the fractional part; a tenth-of-a-centimetre unit captures what falls between the marks.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify that whole-unit readings cannot distinguish lengths between consecutive whole marks, motivating the need for a fractional sub-unit.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses instrument accuracy with the conceptual need for smaller units — the argument is about representation, not ruler quality.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student thinks the problem is about the object being too large, reversing the direction of the difficulty.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student holds a misconception that whole-number centimetre notation is restricted to large lengths rather than understanding it as insufficient for fractional lengths.

inclusivity.support: Let the student re-read the Sonu screw scenario in section 3.1 before answering.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to give a second real-life example where a whole-unit reading would fail to distinguish two different lengths.

exercise.description: Measure the lengths of a pen, sharpener, and an object of the student's choice using a scale; record the measurements in centimetres using tenth notation as modelled in the section.

items.prompt: A unit is divided into 10 equal parts (tenths). Each tenth is then divided into 10 equal parts. How many of these smallest parts make up one whole unit?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option C — 100. Each unit splits into 10 tenths, and each tenth splits into 10 hundredths, giving 10 × 10 = 100 hundredths in one unit.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the two successive divisions: 10 tenths per unit × 10 hundredths per tenth = 100 hundredths per unit.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student counts only the first level of division (tenths), forgetting the second split.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student adds the two levels of division (10 + 10) instead of multiplying them.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student applies a third level of division, confusing hundredths with thousandths.

inclusivity.support: Draw a strip divided first into 10 parts, then shade one part and divide that into 10 — count the total small parts.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask how many thousandths make one unit if each hundredth is further divided into 10 equal parts, and explain the pattern.

exercise.description: How many one-hundredths make one-tenth? Can the folded-paper length also be stated as 4 units and 45 one-hundredths? Explain.

items.prompt: Without using a decimal point or fraction bar, the digit string '305' could represent three different quantities: 305 ones, 30 ones and 5 tenths, or 3 ones and 5 hundredths. Explain, using the place value structure of the base-ten system, why a decimal point is necessary to remove this ambiguity.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: In the base-ten place value system each position is ten times the one to its right. Without a marker, the reader cannot tell which position the digit '3' occupies — hundreds, tens, ones, or tenths — so the same string stands for different quantities. The decimal point fixes the position of the units place, making every other position unambiguous: the digit immediately to its left is ones, the digit immediately to its right is tenths, and so on.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Argue from the base-ten structure: each place is determined relative to the units place, so the decimal point is the anchor that makes the place of every digit determinate.

inclusivity.support: Try the argument with a partner first — say it aloud before writing.
inclusivity.challenge: What if the base were 8 instead of 10 — would a decimal point still work the same way? Explain the difference.

exercise.description: Discuss: could 4 2/10 be written as 42 skipping the fraction denominator? What ambiguity arises? Show three different quantities that could all be denoted '705' without a positional separator.

items.prompt: A cricket scorecard shows a bowler's figures as 4.3 overs. A student says this means the bowler bowled four and three-tenths overs. Explain carefully why this interpretation is wrong, and state what 4.3 overs actually means in cricket. Then give one other everyday context where a dot or decimal-like separator is used but the system is not base ten, and explain why arithmetic on those numbers behaves differently from decimal arithmetic.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: In cricket an over contains 6 balls, not 10. So the separator in '4.3 overs' means 4 complete overs and 3 additional balls — not 3 tenths of an over. If it were a true decimal, 4.3 would mean 4 + 3/10, but here 4.5 would incorrectly suggest 5 balls past 4 overs when the maximum is 6. Arithmetic fails: 4.3 + 0.4 = 4.7 in decimals, but in cricket 3 balls + 4 balls = 7 balls = 1 over and 1 ball, so the result is 5.1, not 4.7. One other context is feet and inches (base 12): 5.9 feet means 5 feet 9 inches, not 5 and 9 tenths feet; adding 5.9 + 0.4 gives 5.13 in feet-inches notation, which equals 6.1 (6 feet 1 inch), not the decimal 6.3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Reason that a decimal-like separator is valid as a base-ten fraction only when the sub-unit divides into exactly 10 parts; cricket overs (6 balls) and feet-inches (12 inches) use different bases, making their notation non-decimal and standard decimal arithmetic inapplicable.

inclusivity.support: Think aloud with a classmate: how many balls are in one over? Does that match the base-ten rule?
inclusivity.challenge: Show with a worked example that adding two 'cricket decimal' figures using ordinary decimal addition gives a wrong answer, and correct it.

exercise.description: Where else can we see 'non-decimal' numbers written with a decimal-like notation? (The cricket overs and feet-inches examples are given; students generate further instances.)

items.prompt: A dragonfly has three body segments. Its head is 1 8/10 units long, its thorax is 4 3/10 units long, and its abdomen is 6 5/10 units long. Find the total body length of the dragonfly. Show your working using both the units-and-tenths column method and the convert-to-tenths method, and confirm that both give the same answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Units-and-tenths method: units: 1 + 4 + 6 = 11; tenths: 8 + 3 + 5 = 16 tenths = 1 unit and 6 tenths. Total = 11 + 1 6/10 = 12 6/10 units. Convert-to-tenths method: 1 8/10 = 18/10; 4 3/10 = 43/10; 6 5/10 = 65/10. Sum = (18 + 43 + 65)/10 = 126/10 = 12 6/10 units. Both methods give 12 6/10 units.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the units parts and the tenths parts separately (regrouping when tenths exceed 9), then verify by converting all to tenths and summing.

inclusivity.support: Draw a number line and mark each segment end-to-end to visualise the total before computing.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the abdomen length to 6 7/10 and recompute; explain how the regrouping step changes.

exercise.description: Find the total length of a honeybee given head = 2 3/10 units, thorax = 5 4/10 units, abdomen = 7 5/10 units.

items.prompt: Three wire segments have lengths 2 7/10 4/100 units, 1 3/100 units, and 4 5/10 units. Find the total length of all three segments. Show your working using the column place value method, aligning tenths with tenths and hundredths with hundredths.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Converting to a common representation: 2 7/10 4/100 = 2 74/100; 1 3/100 = 1 3/100; 4 5/10 = 4 50/100. Column addition: hundredths: 74 + 3 + 50 = 127 hundredths = 1 unit and 27 hundredths; units: 2 + 1 + 4 + 1 (carried) = 8. Total = 8 27/100 units.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Align digits by place (units, tenths, hundredths), add each column right to left, and regroup when a column sum reaches 100 hundredths or 10 tenths.

inclusivity.support: Write each length in a three-column table (units | tenths | hundredths) before adding.
inclusivity.challenge: Now subtract the shortest segment from the total and show your regrouping step explicitly.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 3.3 p.55
exercise.description: In seven groups (a)–(g), identify the longest and shortest length from the given set of tenths and hundredths values, and mark each length on the scale.

items.prompt: A ribbon is 345 mm long. Express this length in centimetres and in metres. Show each conversion step using the unit fractions 1 mm = 0.1 cm and 1 cm = 0.01 m.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Millimetres to centimetres: 1 mm = 0.1 cm, so 345 mm = 345 × 0.1 cm = 34.5 cm. Centimetres to metres: 1 cm = 0.01 m, so 34.5 cm = 34.5 × 0.01 m = 0.345 m. The ribbon is 34.5 cm or 0.345 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the unit fraction 1 mm = 0.1 cm to convert millimetres to centimetres, then 1 cm = 0.01 m to convert centimetres to metres, reading each multiplication as a place value shift.

inclusivity.support: Use the place value table: shifting the decimal point one place left divides by 10 (mm → cm), and another place left divides by 10 again (cm → m).
inclusivity.challenge: Express the same length in kilometres, stating the unit fraction 1 m = 0.001 km and carrying out the conversion.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks for mm ↔ cm conversions: 70 mm = ___ cm; ___ = 0.9 cm; 134 mm = ___; ___ = 203.6 cm.

items.prompt: Which of the following decimal numbers is the greatest?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Option C — 2.910. All four numbers have the same whole-number part (2). Comparing tenths digits: 0, 1, 9, 0 — the largest is 9, so 2.910 is greatest.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare left to right: whole parts are equal; compare tenths digits — the largest tenths digit identifies the greatest number.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be comparing digit counts (2.099 has the digit 9 twice) rather than positional value.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have compared hundredths digits before tenths, reversing left-to-right order.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have misread 2.019 as larger because of its final digit, ignoring the dominant tenths position.

inclusivity.support: Place all four numbers in a tenths-hundredths-thousandths column table and compare column by column from left to right.
inclusivity.challenge: Rearrange all four numbers in descending order and mark each on a number line segment from 2.0 to 3.0.

exercise.description: Which decimal number is greater? (a) 1.23 or 1.32; (b) 3.81 or 13.800; (c) 1.009 or 1.090.

items.prompt: A tailor uses 14.75 m of cloth for shirts and 8.6 m for trousers. She started with a roll of 30 m. How much cloth remains? Show your working in decimal column form, aligning the decimal points.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Total cloth used: 14.75 + 8.60 = 23.35 m. Cloth remaining: 30.00 – 23.35 = 6.65 m. Column subtraction: 30.00 – 23.35 — hundredths: 0 – 5 requires regrouping; tenths: 9 – 3 = 6 (after regrouping); units: 9 – 3 = 6 (after regrouping); tens: 2 – 2 = 0. Remaining cloth = 6.65 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Align decimal points in column form, append trailing zeros so all operands have the same decimal length, then add and subtract with regrouping as in whole-number arithmetic.

inclusivity.support: Sketch the number line: start at 30, step back 14.75, then step back 8.6 to find the remainder.
inclusivity.challenge: If the tailor also needs 3.075 m for a jacket, find the new remainder and check whether Sonu's sum-range claim (section 3.7) applies to the addition step.
